slides.title: One tap, charged twice
slides.tldr: If a reply is lost on the way back, the client sends again; and if the server can't tell the two requests apart, the same payment happens twice.

blocks.body: Rebecca taps "Send" in her app to transfer $50 to Kevin. The server deducts the money, but the reply gets lost in the network on its way back. All Rebecca sees is a spinning wheel, so she taps again. To the server this is a brand-new request, and it deducts another $50.

blocks.caption: One intention, two requests, charged twice

actors.label: Rebecca's phone
actors.tip: Rebecca wants to send $50 exactly once. With no reply, she taps again.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Treats every POST as new work. It has nothing that links this request to the earlier one.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Does what the server tells it to; if the same transfer arrives twice, it writes it twice.

messages.label: Success (reply lost on the way)
messages.tip: The work is done, but the news never reached Rebecca. From her side it looks as if nothing happened.

messages.note: No reply, so she taps again

messages.label: Deduct $50 again
messages.tip: The server has no idea this is the second attempt at the same job.
Rebecca wanted to send $50. No code threw an exception, yet the books are wrong.

blocks.body: Any request you send once can arrive twice. Build every write so that arriving twice still happens once.

aside.title: Who else sends again?
aside.body: It isn't only impatient fingers. A mobile app's auto-retry, a load balancer, a queue worker, a payment gateway's webhook: all of them send again when no reply comes back. Duplicate requests are not an edge case, they are an everyday event.

items.meaning: Sending the same request again because no reply came back.
A request for the same job that has reached the server more than once.

check.q: The server did deduct the money correctly the first time. Why did it deduct a second time?
check.a: The reply was lost, so Rebecca never learned the job was done and sent it again. And the server had nothing that told it the two requests were the same job.

slides.title: The check number: one check can't be cashed twice
slides.tldr: The client sends a unique key with each job; the server records the key, and when the same key comes back it returns the earlier reply.

blocks.title: The bank's checkbook
blocks.body: Every page in a checkbook has its own printed number. When the bank pays out, it writes that number in its register. If the same check turns up at the counter again, the cashier doesn't pay a second time. She checks the register and says, "This was already paid, here's the receipt." An **idempotency key** is a request's check number.

blocks.caption: The first time the work is done; the second time only the stored reply comes back

nodes.label: Vue app
nodes.tip: The owner of the checkbook. It generates a new UUID for every new job and sends the same one again on a retry.

nodes.label: API
nodes.tip: Before touching anything, it checks the key in the register: a new key means do the work, a known key means hand back the receipt.

nodes.label: Key register
nodes.tip: The ledger of which key got which reply. The same key can't be entered here twice.

nodes.label: The real work
nodes.tip: The job that causes harm if it runs twice. For one key it runs exactly once.

edges.label: The client sends an Idempotency-Key with the request
The server enters the key in the register: it is new
Since the key is new, it does the real work once
It stores the reply next to the key
The reply goes out, but say it gets lost on the way
The client sends again with the same key
Known key: no new work, the stored reply is returned

blocks.body: A job is **idempotent** if doing it once or ten times gives the same final result. `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are naturally like that; `POST` is not, which is why `POST` needs this key.

items.meaning: An operation whose end result is the same whether you do it once or many times.
A unique identity for one job, usually a UUID; the client makes it and sends it in a header.

aside.body: New job = new key. Another try at the same job = the same key.

items.label: Which errors are safe to retry

check.q: When a second request arrives with the same idempotency key, what does the server do, and what does it not do?
check.a: It does not repeat the real work. It returns the stored reply from the first time, exactly as it was.

slides.title: Building the register: key, fingerprint and stored reply
slides.tldr: Keep one table with (scope, key) unique, and store the request's fingerprint and the response; the controller takes the key from the header and hands it to a guard.

blocks.body: Each line of the register holds four things: whose key it is (the **scope**), the key itself, the request's **fingerprint** (a hash of the body, like the amount written on a check), and the reply from the first time. A unique constraint on `(scope, idem_key)` is what guarantees the same check number never gets entered twice.

blocks.code:
#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'idempotency_key')]
#[ORM\UniqueConstraint(name: 'uniq_scope_key', columns: ['scope', 'idem_key'])]
class IdempotencyKey
{
    #[ORM\Id, ORM\GeneratedValue, ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

    #[ORM\Column(length: 80)]
    private string $scope;                  // whose key: 'user:42'

    #[ORM\Column(length: 36)]
    private string $idemKey;                // the UUID the client sent

    #[ORM\Column(length: 64)]
    private string $fingerprint;            // sha256 of the request

    #[ORM\Column(nullable: true)]
    private ?int $responseStatus = null;    // filled in when the work is done

    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::TEXT, nullable: true)]
    private ?string $responseBody = null;

    #[ORM\Column]
    private \DateTimeImmutable $createdAt;  // so old keys can be purged
}

marks.tip: The backbone of the whole scheme. The database itself refuses a second row for the same key in the same scope, even if your code gets it wrong.
If the same key comes with a different amount or recipient, this hash won't match and we turn the request away.
A request that moves money is not accepted without a key. Making the header mandatory means no client can forget it.
The fingerprint: a hash of the method, path and raw body. An honest retry sends exactly the same bytes, so the hash matches.
The real work is passed in as a closure. The guard decides whether to run it or return the stored reply.

items: Keep keys for at least 24 hours, longer than a client can keep retrying. Then run a job that deletes old rows by `created_at`.
Put the user id in the scope. Otherwise one person's key could return another person's stored reply.

items.meaning: A hash of the request's contents; it exposes a different request arriving under the same key.
Who the key belongs to, usually the logged-in user or API client.

check.q: Without the fingerprint column, which mistake would go unnoticed?
check.a: A different request under the same key (say $500 instead of $50). The server couldn't tell, and would return the old $50 reply as a "success".

slides.title: Claim, work, store the reply: in one transaction
slides.tldr: Insert the key row, do the real work and store the reply in one transaction; if the INSERT affects 0 rows, replay the stored reply without doing the work.

blocks.body: The guard does three things, all in **one transaction**: insert the key row, run the real work, write the reply onto the row. If anything breaks halfway, all three roll back together. The key disappears too, so the client can safely try again. If the same key arrives twice at once, the unique constraint makes the second request wait, and then it simply gets the stored reply.

marks.tip: Everything inside this closure is one transaction. If an exception is thrown, everything rolls back, key row included.
No SELECT first, just INSERT. If another running transaction holds the same key, the database makes you wait here, then returns 0 rows.
0 rows means someone else already finished this key's work. The real work is not touched again.
If someone brings a changed amount under the same check number, the bank sends them away. Here that is a 422: the client has a bug and needs to hear about it.

blocks.caption: When the same key arrives twice at once, the work still happens once

actors.label: Request A
actors.tip: The first attempt. It manages to insert the key row first, so it is the one that does the work.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Thanks to the unique constraint, it holds back a second INSERT of the same key until the first one's outcome is final.

actors.label: Request B
actors.tip: A second attempt with the same key (a double-click, say) that arrived before A finished.

messages.note: B waits: A has not committed yet
messages.tip: The database can't know whether A will commit or roll back, so it makes B wait.

messages.note: B gives the same reply without working
messages.tip: The money moved once, yet both requests got the same "success" reply.

blocks.body: Never SELECT first and INSERT later. INSERT straight away: the unique constraint is the judge.

items: If you SELECT "does the key exist?" and then INSERT, two requests can both see "no" and both do the work.
If the key row is committed first in a separate transaction, a failure in the work leaves the key stuck, and no retry can ever do the job.
On MySQL, use `INSERT IGNORE` in place of `ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING`. It also hides other insert errors, so validate the input first.
The price: the key row stays locked until COMMIT, so a duplicate request waits that long. Keep the work inside short.
If the work calls an outside gateway, pass the same key to it too. Then you also have to deal with the [[payments/unknown-outcomes/timeout-not-failure|"we don't know" state]].

check.q: If the server crashes halfway through the work, what happens to the key row, and why is that good?
check.a: The row was in the same transaction as the work, so it is rolled back and vanishes. The next retry can then do the whole job from scratch, exactly once.

slides.title: A new key on every try: the classic mistake
slides.tldr: A key belongs to the user's intention, not to an attempt: the same key on a retry, a new key when the form changes.

blocks.body: However careful the server is, if the client makes a fresh key on every click, each retry looks like a new check and the money is deducted again. Tie the key to the user's **intention**: "$50 to Kevin" is one intention, no matter how many times the button is pressed. If the recipient or amount changes, that's a new intention and gets a new key.

marks.tip: The key is created at the moment of sending. So on a second click or a retry the server sees a completely new key and does the work again.
The key is created once, when the form opens. However many times send() runs after that, the same key goes out.
If the recipient or amount changes and you keep the old key, the fingerprint won't match and the server returns 422. So a new intention gets a new key.
The server has clearly said yes or no, so the matter is settled. The next transfer should get a new key.
A network error or a 5xx means "we don't know". The key stays unchanged, so tapping again lets the server recognize the same job.

items: Disabling the button is good practice but not enough: a page refresh, two tabs or an auto-retry get past it. Only the server's key check stops those.
`crypto.randomUUID()` works only over HTTPS or on localhost.
If the job should survive a page reload, keep the key in `sessionStorage`.

aside.body: Make the key when the form opens, not when you send.

check.q: The user changes the amount from $50 to $70 and taps "Send" again. Should the key stay the same? Why?
check.a: No, make a new key. Changing the amount is a new intention. With the old key the fingerprint wouldn't match and the server would answer 422.

slides.title: Every write: what if it arrives twice?
slides.tldr: Not every write needs a key: some are naturally idempotent, some are covered by a unique constraint, and the rest are made safe with an idempotency key.

blocks.body: An idempotency key is not the only tool. In front of every write endpoint, queue handler and webhook, ask one question: "What happens if this arrives twice?" Then pick the simplest approach in the table below that fits.

blocks.caption: How each kind of write becomes safe against duplicates

rows.tip: Setting the same value ten times gives the same result. So "set this value" writes are always safer than "increase/decrease" ones.
Put the business rule into the database. The second attempt hits the constraint, so no separate key table is needed.
The same user can legitimately send the same amount twice, so you can't spot a duplicate from the data. You need the client's key.
A queue can deliver the same message more than once. The handler first checks whether it has handled this id before.
If the gateway gets no reply, it sends the same news again. Keep a unique constraint on the event id and ignore the second one.

blocks.title: Idempotency key checklist
items: The client makes the key, once per job; a retry reuses the same key.
Key row, real work and reply: all in one transaction.
Unique constraint on `(scope, key)`; never SELECT first and then INSERT.
Same key with a different fingerprint gets 422; keep keys for at least 24 hours.

aside.body: Wherever you can, write "set", not "increase": setting twice does no harm.

check.q: Of `balance = balance - 50` and `status = 'paid'`, which UPDATE is dangerous if it runs twice, and why?
check.a: The first: it takes off another $50 each time. The second sets the same value, so running it twice leaves the same result.

slides.title: Who sent this "paid" message?
slides.tldr: A webhook is a POST that arrives at your URL from outside; trust it without checking the seal and anyone can fake a "paid" call and get an order for free.

blocks.body: Ryan's online store takes payment and then ships the order. When the money arrives, the payment gateway POSTs to a URL on Ryan's server to say "order 77 paid". That call is a **webhook**. The catch is that the URL is open to the whole internet. Anyone who finds the URL can POST "order 77 paid" to it, and Ryan's server believes it without any check and ships the goods.

blocks.caption: A fake webhook marks an order paid with no money

actors.label: A stranger
actors.tip: Not the gateway, but he can POST to the same URL pretending to be the gateway, because the URL is open to everyone.

actors.label: Ryan's server
actors.tip: The code behind the webhook URL. It takes the body at its word without asking who sent it.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Writes whatever the server tells it; even a fake message becomes the truth.

messages.note: No money came, order is paid
messages.tip: The database now holds a lie. The goods will leave, and no money will arrive.

blocks.body: Whatever a webhook body says, until the seal checks out it is just the word of a stranger.

aside.body: A webhook URL is not a secret. Hiding the URL doesn't make you safe: you have to prove mathematically that each call really came from the gateway.

items.meaning: A POST that another system sends to your URL by itself when something happens.
Sending a fake request while pretending to be someone else.

check.q: Is a very long, random webhook URL secure enough by itself? Why not?
check.a: No. A URL can leak through logs, proxies or email. So you verify the signature of every call; keeping the URL secret is not enough.

slides.title: The sealed package: HMAC signatures
slides.tldr: The gateway sends a signature: an HMAC of the body and timestamp under a shared secret. The server builds the same hash itself to compare, and rejects old timestamps.

blocks.title: The delivery company's sealed package
blocks.body: The delivery company and Ryan share a secret stamp that nobody else has. The company looks at what's inside the package and the date, then stamps a seal. Ryan makes a seal of his own with the same stamp and compares. If the contents change, the seal won't match. And if last month's sealed package turns up again today, he sends it back because of the date.

blocks.caption: Seal matches: do the work. No match: reject

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.tip: Runs HMAC-SHA256 over the body and timestamp with the shared secret to make the seal (signature), and sends it in a header.

nodes.label: Webhook endpoint
nodes.tip: Checks the seal and the timestamp before doing anything else.

nodes.label: Seal is good
nodes.tip: The signature matches and the timestamp is fresh. Now it is safe to store the event.

nodes.label: Seal is wrong
nodes.tip: If the signature doesn't match, or the timestamp is more than five minutes old, the request is dropped.

edges.label: The gateway sends the body with a seal of body and timestamp in a header
The server builds a seal with its own secret and compares: they match
If the seal doesn't match or the timestamp is old, it rejects the call
When all is well, it quickly replies 200

items.meaning: A hash made from a secret key plus a message; without the key you can't produce the same hash.
Capturing a genuine, sealed request and sending it again later.

aside.body: Seal = HMAC(secret, timestamp + body). The timestamp is inside the seal, which is why it can't be changed.

check.q: If someone captures a genuine sealed request and resends it two days later, the signature is still valid. How do you stop that?
check.a: The timestamp is part of the seal. The server checks whether the timestamp is more than five minutes away from the current time, and if so it rejects the request even though the seal is valid.

slides.title: Verify, store, then reply 200
slides.tldr: Check the seal with hash_hmac and hash_equals on the raw body, store the event and hand it to Messenger, and return 200 fast.

blocks.body: Keep two rules in mind. First, verify the seal against the **raw body**, not the array you get after `json_decode`, because even a change in whitespace changes the hash. Second, the gateway waits only briefly for your reply, so don't do slow work: verify, store, and answer 200.

marks.tip: The secret does not live in code or in git; it comes from an env var or Symfony secrets.
Anything older than five minutes is treated as a replay and dropped. The timestamp sits inside the seal, so nobody can alter it.
Not a plain ===. hash_equals stops attackers from guessing the hash character by character by measuring response time (a timing attack).
getContent() returns exactly the bytes that arrived. This is what the seal must be checked against.
A unique constraint on event_id. If the gateway sends the same event twice, the second one creates no new row.
A worker will do the real work later. Here we only wrote the event into the ledger.

blocks.title: Which reply, and when
items: 200: the seal is good and the event is stored, even if the event type is one you don't recognize.
400/401: the seal is wrong. Retrying from the gateway would not help.
500: you couldn't write to the database. The gateway will then retry on its own.
Most gateways retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff for hours or days. Returning 500 is how you ask for that retry.
When you rotate the secret, accept both the old and the new one for a short while.

check.q: Why does the seal check need the raw body rather than the `json_decode`d array? And why is slow work kept out of the controller?
check.a: Re-encoding an array can change the bytes, and then the hash won't match. And if slow work takes too long, the gateway times out and sends the same event again.

slides.title: It will arrive twice, and out of order
slides.tldr: Webhooks are delivered at least once and in no guaranteed order; the handler must block duplicates by event id, and a state machine must stop old news from moving a payment backwards.

blocks.body: A gateway that gets no reply sends the same event again, so seeing one event twice is normal. And `succeeded` can arrive before `pending`, because retries scramble the order. The easiest mistake is to set the status and send the email right in the controller. The handler below fixes that, and its `TooEarly` branch (the next slide explains it) keeps an event that arrives too soon from being lost.

marks.tip: If a pending event arrives late, it turns a succeeded payment back into pending. Writing the status directly is dangerous.
If the same event arrives twice, the customer gets two receipts, and without keeping the gateway's copy you can't recognize the duplicate.
You can only claim it while processed_at IS NULL. Even if two workers arrive together, only one updates 1 row.
0 rows means someone else already handled it. Just return: no exception, or Messenger would retry.
The payment status isn't set directly here; the state machine checks the transition is valid and only then changes it.
The payment is not ready for this event yet. Throwing rolls back the claim above, so the event stays unprocessed and can be retried.

blocks.body: Assume both about webhooks: the same event will come more than once, and the order will not be right.

items: Don't rely on order. Let the state machine accept only forward transitions, drop old news, and never move a status backwards.
When in doubt, don't trust the event's data: ask the gateway's API for the payment's current state.

items.label: Valid transitions and the state machine
Making the same job safe to repeat

check.q: When a duplicate event reaches the worker handler, how many rows does `UPDATE ... processed_at IS NULL` change, and what does the handler do then?
check.a: The first time, 1 row, so the work runs. For a duplicate, 0 rows, so the handler quietly returns and does nothing more.

slides.title: An early event must not be thrown away
slides.tldr: If the payment is not ready for an event yet, rejecting it and marking it processed loses it for good. Roll back and retry; drop only events the payment has already moved past.

blocks.body: Ryan's app calls the gateway, which charges the card and fires a `payment.succeeded` webhook at once. But the reply that carries the gateway's payment id is still on its way, so Ryan's row has no gateway id yet. The handler looks the payment up, finds nothing, and returns quietly, with the event already marked processed. A second later the id is saved, and nobody will ever send `succeeded` again. The customer has paid, and the order waits forever.

blocks.caption: The same early event, thrown away versus kept for later

columns.title: Drop and mark done
items: `succeeded` arrives before our row has its gateway id
No payment found, so the handler returns and the event counts as processed
The id is saved a second later
No event comes again: the payment is stuck in `pending`
columns.tip: The handler treats every rejected event as old news, including one that is only early.

columns.title: Roll back and retry
items: `succeeded` arrives before our row has its gateway id
The payment is behind the event, so the claim is rolled back
Messenger retries after 2, 4, 8 seconds
By then the id is saved, `succeed` is legal and gets applied
columns.tip: The handler asks one more question: is the payment behind this event, or already past it?

marks.tip: No row for this gateway id yet also means the event is early, not wrong.
The state machine said no. Now we find out why.
Behind the event: wait. At or past it: the news is old and safe to drop.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        failure_transport: failed
        transports:
            async:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                retry_strategy:
                    max_retries: 6
                    delay: 2000        # 2s, then 4s, 8s, 16s, 32s, 64s
                    multiplier: 2
            failed: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=failed'

marks.tip: Six retries cover about two minutes, plenty for a payment row that is a second late.
An event that is still early after the last retry goes here for a human, instead of vanishing.

blocks.body: Drop an event only when the payment is already past it. If the payment is behind it, roll back and retry.

use: Events that can overtake the write they depend on
Any handler that marks work done before the work is accepted
avoid: Events that will never become valid (a payment you never created): retries only add noise, so let them reach the failure transport quickly

items: Retries cost delay, not correctness. For a stuck event after the last retry, the [[payments/unknown-outcomes/timeout-not-failure|sweeper]] asks the gateway for the payment's real state.

check.q: A `succeeded` event arrives but no payment has that gateway id yet. Drop it, or roll back and retry? What about a `failed` event for a payment that is already `succeeded`?
check.a: Roll back and retry the first: the payment is behind the event, and no second `succeeded` will ever come. Drop the second: the payment is already past it, so it is old news.

slides.title: A status that anyone can write anything into
slides.tldr: If a payment's status is a plain string that any code can set, a failed payment gets refunded and a successful one slips back to pending.

blocks.body: In Ryan's app, the `payments` table has a `status` column, and ten places in the code call `setStatus('...')`. One day a stale webhook turns up late and flips a `succeeded` payment back to `pending`. Another day a support agent hits refund on a `failed` payment, and money that never arrived goes back out. No exception, no log, just wrong books.

blocks.caption: What a plain string status allows, and what a state machine allows

columns.title: Anything can be written
items: succeeded → pending (from stale news)
failed → refunded (no money ever came)
No way to tell who changed it, or when
columns.tip: Any code can set any status from anywhere, so nothing stands in the way of a wrong change.

columns.title: Only legal paths work
items: No way from succeeded back to pending
No way forward from failed
Every change is logged
columns.tip: Every change goes through a named transition, and an illegal one is rejected on the spot.

blocks.body: A payment's status is never written directly. It changes only through a named, legal transition.

aside.title: The train ticket rules
aside.body: A ticket that has been refunded never becomes valid again, and a ticket that was never bought can't be refunded. These rules aren't memorized by the clerk at the counter; they are built into the system itself.

items.meaning: The condition something is in right now, such as pending or succeeded.
A named, legal path from one state to another.

check.q: If some code mistakenly tries to run `refund` on a `failed` payment, what happens when a state machine is in place?
check.a: There is no transition called refund out of failed, so it can't run. The code throws an exception or `can()` returns false, and no money goes back.

slides.title: The ticket's life: states, transitions and terminals
slides.tldr: Draw the payment's legal states and the legal transitions between them up front; nothing leaves failed or refunded.

blocks.title: The life of a train ticket
blocks.body: It starts with a booking request: the money is being collected (pending), then the ticket is issued (succeeded) or canceled because no money came (failed). An issued ticket can be returned for a refund (refunded). But a canceled or refunded ticket has nothing more to do. Those end positions are called **terminal states**.

blocks.caption: A payment's five states and four legal transitions

nodes.label: created
nodes.tip: The payment has been made as a record, but not yet sent to the gateway.

nodes.label: pending
nodes.tip: The gateway has been told. Until it answers, we don't know whether the money came.

nodes.label: succeeded
nodes.tip: The money has arrived. From here only the refund path is open.

nodes.label: failed
nodes.tip: The money did not come. This is an end state; there are no transitions out of it.

nodes.label: refunded
nodes.tip: The money has gone back. Also an end state; once fully refunded there is nothing more to do.

edges.label: submit
edges.tip: The payment is sent to the gateway.

edges.label: succeed
edges.tip: The gateway reports that the money came.

edges.label: fail
edges.tip: The gateway reports that the money did not come.

edges.label: refund
edges.tip: The money is returned. This is possible only from succeeded.

blocks.title: What this diagram gives us
items: There is no direct `created → succeeded`: you can't call a payment successful without asking the gateway whether the money came.
Nothing leaves `failed` or `refunded`, so stale news can't change them.
Complications like partial refunds live in [[workflows/refunds-reversals/edited-the-amount|a separate segment]].

aside.body: Draw the diagram first, then the code. A path that's not in the diagram is not in the code.

use: Anything with a few clear states: a payment, an order, a contract
When stale or late events must be rejected
avoid: Where there are only two states (active/inactive) and no rules

check.q: The diagram has no arrow from `refunded` back to `succeeded`. Why is that deliberate?
check.a: If a refunded payment went back to "succeeded", the books would be wrong. To take money again, you create a new payment.

slides.title: Putting the diagram into code with Symfony Workflow
slides.tldr: Describe places and transitions under framework.workflows with type: state_machine; then calling can() and apply() rejects an illegal change on the spot.

blocks.body: In the Symfony Workflow component, the diagram is written under `framework.workflows`. `type: state_machine` says a payment is in exactly one state at a time. `marking_store` says which property holds the status, so the entity's `status` field is updated for you. After that, you just ask with `can()` and change with `apply()`.

marks.tip: state_machine means exactly one state at a time. (The workflow type can hold several places at once; we don't want that for a payment.)
Every transition is written to the log: which payment, and from which state to which.
The workflow uses Payment::getStatus()/setStatus(). The status field on the entity is a string.
If the parameter is named paymentStateMachine, Symfony automatically injects the state machine called payment.
can() asks: "is there a path with this name out of the current state?" If false, the state is left unchanged.
apply() changes the status. So far only in memory; you need a flush to write it to the database.

items.desc: Add the component if it's missing

items.cmd: php bin/console workflow:dump payment | dot -Tpng -o payment.png

items: You can hook in work before or after a transition with an event listener: `#[AsEventListener(event: 'workflow.payment.completed.succeed')]`.
A guard adds conditions: `guard: 'is_granted("ROLE_ADMIN")'`.
A `false` only says "not legal right now". It can mean old news (drop it) or an event that came early (retry it); the caller decides. See [[payments/webhooks/early-event|early events]].

check.q: Does calling `apply()` change the status in the database? And what does `can()` tell you?
check.a: No. apply() changes only the in-memory object; the database changes when you flush. can() tells you whether that transition is legal from the current state.

slides.title: Two workers at once: can() is not enough
slides.tldr: can() and apply() work in memory; if two workers read the same pending payment together, both think they are legal. Use a database lock or a conditional UPDATE to make the change atomic.

blocks.body: Say a `succeed` webhook and a `fail` webhook arrive almost together, picked up by two different workers. Both read the payment, both see status `pending`, and `can()` is true for both. One writes `succeeded`, and the other writes `failed` over it. The diagram was right, but it was fooled in the gap between reading and writing.

marks.tip: No lock. Another worker has read the same row at the same time.
Both flushes succeed. The later one writes without knowing what the earlier one did.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Another worker trying to read this row waits until this transaction finishes.
The second worker will now read a status that is no longer pending, so can() returns false.
The transition history is written in the same transaction, so "who changed what, when" is never lost.

blocks.body: Checking that a transition is legal and changing the status happen under one lock, in one transaction.

use: Pessimistic lock: when several actors are likely to reach the same payment at once
Optimistic lock (`#[ORM\Version]`): when conflicts are rare and retrying is easy
avoid: Relying on can() alone with no lock

items.label: This transition inside a webhook handler

check.q: After waiting for the lock, what does the second worker see, and what does it do?
check.a: Once the first worker commits, it sees that the status is no longer pending. So `can()` returns false, and it returns without changing anything.

slides.title: A timeout, and nobody knows whether the money moved
slides.tldr: When a gateway call times out, it may have succeeded, failed or be unknown; treat a timeout as failure and retry, and the customer is charged twice.

blocks.body: Ryan's app tells the gateway, "charge $120 to Rachel's card." The gateway takes the money, but the network jams on the way back, and after 5 seconds Ryan's app gets a timeout. The app assumes "failed", marks the payment `failed` and tells Rachel to try again. Rachel taps again, and $120 is deducted twice.

blocks.caption: Treating a timeout as failure charges the money twice

actors.label: Ryan's app
actors.tip: Calls the gateway. When no reply comes, it decides for itself, and that is the mistake.

actors.label: Gateway
actors.tip: The real owner of the charge. It knows what actually happened, but couldn't tell the app.

actors.label: Rachel
actors.tip: The customer. She believes whatever the app shows her.

messages.tip: The work was done properly, but the app doesn't know yet.
A timeout only says no reply came. It doesn't say whether the work failed.

blocks.body: A timeout doesn't mean failure, it means "I don't know". Until you know, say neither failed nor succeeded.

aside.body: Over a network, a job takes two steps: going out and the reply coming back. Lose it at either step and the app sees the same thing from outside: silence.

items.meaning: The state of not knowing whether the work happened, usually after a timeout or a dropped connection.

check.q: After a timeout, how many outcomes are possible, and which one did the app wrongly choose?
check.a: Three: success, failure or unknown. The app treated unknown as failure, yet the money had actually been taken.

slides.title: No confirmation, but the balance went down
slides.tldr: Give the unknown state its own place (pending), then take your time asking the gateway for the truth or wait for its webhook; never guess.

blocks.title: A payment app charge, but no confirmation
blocks.body: Rachel pays at a restaurant with a payment app like Venmo, but the cashier's screen shows no confirmation. The cashier doesn't say "I didn't get it", and doesn't say "I got it" either. She says "hold on", then checks the transaction ID in the payment app. That "hold on" is **pending**, and checking the app is a **status query**; the real truth lives in the payment provider's ledger.

blocks.caption: When you don't know, stay pending, then ask the gateway

nodes.label: Our app
nodes.tip: Sends the charge, and when no reply comes it makes no decision. It waits and verifies.

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.tip: Only this ledger can say whether the money was actually taken, not our database.

nodes.label: pending
nodes.tip: The unknown state's own home. It is neither failed nor succeeded, so no wrong decision gets made.

nodes.label: succeeded / failed
nodes.tip: The payment arrives here only after the gateway's real answer.

edges.label: The app sends the charge and no reply comes (timeout)
The app keeps the payment pending and does not call it failed
Later it asks the gateway for the status, using the same reference
The gateway gives the real result: succeeded or failed
The app moves the payment to match that result

blocks.body: There are three ways to learn the result: the gateway's **webhook** arrives, you run a **status query** yourself, or a regular **reconciliation** job goes through the stuck pending payments and matches them up. Keep all three, because any one of them can fail.

items.meaning: The ledger whose word is final; here, the gateway.
Comparing your own ledger with an outside one, then finding and fixing mismatches.

check.q: If you skip the pending state and set failed straight after a timeout, what information is lost?
check.a: You lose the fact that the result was really unknown. If the gateway later reports success, nothing tells us how to correct a payment we marked failed.

slides.title: Stay pending, and retry with the same key
slides.tldr: Commit the payment as pending before calling the gateway; on a transport error or 5xx, don't fail it but verify later; and on a retry, send the same idempotency key.

marks.tip: A new key every time means the gateway sees each attempt as separate work; a retry will charge again.
Every exception is treated as failure. On a timeout the payment stays failed even if the money was taken.
Pending is committed before the call. Even if we crash, the ledger shows that a call was in flight.
The key was made once, when the payment was created, so every attempt sends this same key.
TransportExceptionInterface also covers timeouts. We don't set failed here; we only schedule a check for later.
5xx, 408 and 429 mean the gateway hasn't given a final word. Any other 4xx is a clear "no".
The check runs 30 seconds later, giving the gateway time to finish the work.

blocks.body: On a retry, always the same idempotency key. A new key means new work.

items: HttpClient is lazy: the real error appears only when you call `getStatusCode()` or `getContent()`, not on `request()`.
Always set a `timeout`. Without one, your own app can hang forever.

check.q: When does `charge()` mark the payment `failed`, and when does it not?
check.a: Only for a clear rejection (4xx, other than 408 and 429). On a timeout, a dropped connection, 408, 429 or 5xx it stays pending and is checked later.

slides.title: Ask for the truth: status queries and the sweeper
slides.tldr: A CheckPaymentStatus handler asks the gateway by reference and settles the payment; a periodic sweeper picks up old pending ones and sends them back for checking.

blocks.body: Verification runs in two ways: once, on time (a delayed message), and through a regular sweeper for pending payments whose time has run out. Both ask the gateway by `reference`, and neither does anything on its own guess.

marks.tip: If it's no longer pending there is nothing to do: the webhook came. This check makes the handler idempotent.
We search by our own reference, because we may never have received the gateway's id.
404 means the call never reached the gateway. Then sending the charge again with the same key is safe.
If the gateway itself still says "processing", we wait: ask again 60 seconds later.
A Symfony Scheduler attribute. You need to run a worker: messenger:consume scheduler_default.
Pending for more than 15 minutes means neither the webhook nor the earlier query worked. Pick these up again.

items.desc: The worker that runs Scheduler tasks

items: If a payment stays pending for a long time (say 24 hours), alert a person. Don't keep retrying on your own forever.
Each status query is a call to the gateway. A few hundred stuck payments every 10 minutes is fine; thousands every minute can hit its rate limit.

check.q: If a status query makes the gateway say "I don't recognize this reference" (404), what is the safe move, and why?
check.a: Send the charge again with the same idempotency key. The call never reached the gateway, and if it did arrive late, the same key stops the work from happening a second time.
